beta_new: Opens with a layback off a large clean flake into a long left-facing corner system with finger cracks, crosses right below a roof into a splitter crack to a mid-route ledge, then a second roof leads to a hand crack and stemming corners with a hard exit, topping out via a deep summit chimney.

moves.from: ; protection is cams and nuts to 3 inches throughout

beta_new: This is the standard and essentially only documented way up Plummer Peak. Hike the maintained Pinnacle Peak Trail from Reflection Lakes through forest and talus to the saddle between Pinnacle and Plummer Peaks (~5,950 ft). At the saddle, leave the maintained tread and follow a well-worn boot path that curves right/west and then climbs the north side/ridge of Plummer, passing a seasonal tarn, to top out on the small (50x15 ft) summit block. The final ~400 ft above the saddle is loose, sometimes steep Class 2 terrain with a couple of short hands-on steps; a few well-placed trees aid the last moves. No rope or protection is used on this route.

The first pitch is the technical and psychological crux: sustained 5.9 face/dike climbing off the bergschrund with roughly 40 feet of essentially unprotectable climbing before gear appears around half height. Confident, composed 5.9 face-climbing ability and comfort well above sparse pro are essential before committing to the lead.

A series of corners, overhangs, and slabs to the top of Osprey Wall with excellent crystal pocket holds; protection is a mix of bolts and natural gear, with the third pitch fully bolted. Pitch 1 ("First Flight," 5.6) is a bolted slab ending in a chute; P2 (5.9+) climbs a right-facing corner with a roof and bolted slab; P3 (5.10c, "the money pitch") features roof systems and an arete on white marbled rock; P4 (5.9) follows a corner ramp becoming an open book (with two variations); P5 (5.10c) finishes on an arete.

A granite ridge climb with lichened overlaps, gardened dirt-filled cracks and clean tactile smears on low-angle granite; the crux comes late, on pitch 9, with an S-curved crack and bulge with smearing moves to chain anchors.

moves.from: Modern bolted anchors added in 2023 made the route rappel-able for the first time.

beta_new: Primus Peak's difficulty lies almost entirely in its remoteness and glacier approach rather than technical climbing. From this side the summit itself is class 2-3 snow and talus above the North Klawatti Glacier, reached after a short rock step at the McAllister-Klawatti notch. Most parties treat it as a 3-4 day trip with a high camp near Klawatti Col. A harder 'North Ridge' variant (5.6 trad, loose and exposed) exists for parties wanting technical climbing.

A wiggly crack in mossy rock. Climb through a moss-covered corner ledge, then mossy face climbing to a moss-covered summit jug. Bolts mentioned in older descriptions were not visible on a recent visit, likely buried under moss -- treat as a natural-gear/trad line with a chain anchor at the top.

moves.from: treat as a natural-gear/trad line with a chain anchor at the top

beta_new: P1 ('The Onramp', 5.5) romps up an easy 5th-class left-leaning slab to a pine-covered ledge. P2 ('The Superflake', 5.9) climbs a steep flake system tapering to an airy spire. P3 (5.9) steps right into a dihedral. P4 (5.10-) tackles a slightly overhanging crack with good gear to an angled ledge. P5 ('Gemini Cracks', 5.10) offers tight, baggy hand cracks with a traverse option. P6 ('Sail Headwall', 5.11) finishes on an elegant, slightly overhanging crack progressing from thin fingers to off-width.

From the end of the maintained Pyramid Lake Trail, an unmaintained but cairned climbers' path continues up the long south ridge through forest, brush, and boulder fields to timberline. The route then traverses below steep cliffs on the peak's east side (prone to sliding) before climbing to the saddle between Pinnacle and Pyramid Peaks. From the saddle it's an easy walk to Pyramid's summit. The route's overall difficulty is Class 3 scrambling, though most of the elevation gain is Class 1-2 hiking with only short harder sections.

From the saddle between Vesper and Wolf Peak, an obvious ledge system cuts across the north face at roughly 5,800 ft, starting at a small notch overlooking the Vesper Glacier. The climbing is sustained low-5th-class rock with the crux exposed traverse pitch reported on pitch 5 (some parties also flag a 5.7 slab on pitch 2); belays are a mix of fixed (bolted/pin) anchors and gear anchors atop pitches 1 and 3. Popular enough that other Vesper lines (e.g. True Grit) are sometimes used as a less-crowded backup.

moves.from: No rappels are needed — parties walk off.

beta_new: Typically approached via Easy Pass and Fisher Creek to a high camp on Mesahchie's south shoulder, then done as either a long single-day push (~13-14 hrs car-to-car) or a 2-day trip across the four 8,000+ ft summits (Kitling Peak to the east is sometimes added). No roped rock climbing is required, but the terrain is loose, exposed, and route-finding-intensive.

From the Libby Lake Trailhead, hike the well-graded Libby Creek/Libby Lake Trail roughly 5.1–5.5 miles and about 3,185–3,210 ft of gain to Libby Lake (~7,618–7,640 ft). From the lake, locate the loose talus gully that accesses the east-west-oriented ridge (some parties report two gully options near the lake's south end; the standard line rises about 900 ft). The gully is loose and rockfall-prone — favor the climber's-left wall for firmer rock and to reduce hazard to parties below. Once on the ridge crest, an exposed Class 2–3 scramble of roughly half a mile leads toward the summit block, which has a short, unavoidable, no-fall Class 4 move (some reports mention a small tunnel feature en route). USGS topo maps mislabel the western "Libby" summit as the high point (8,580 ft); the true, higher summit is the eastern peak at 8,572 ft. The true east summit is also known as Corax Peak; a separate, lower point sits just west of the main summit saddle. Strong parties often continue the ridge traverse north to Hoodoo Peak, which adds a long exposed Class 4 section and a 5.7 overhanging boulder problem best protected with a short rope.

The final 1,000-1,100 feet ascends the west-facing slope at 30-40 degrees inclination. Most loose rock has been removed by frequent traffic. South-facing sections feature more solid red volcanic slabs. Winter ascents are possible with snow coverage on the southwest ridge when avalanche conditions are stable.

moves.from: Approach via Pacific Crest Trail north from Exit 52, following Commonwealth Creek trail to the base of the mountain.

beta_new: 5 bolts to chains.

moves.from: Approach to Megadike North 1.1-1.2 miles past Middle Point Ridge Trailhead.

beta_new: Long moderate slabby arete. Bolts to anchors at top.

From a high camp at roughly 7,500 ft on the lower ridge, the route follows a long, stable, lightly-vegetated boulder ridge to the North Summit, from which two rappels on the west side regain the ridge crest. Beyond, two main gendarmes block easy passage; each is climbed at about 5.1-5.2. The line appears sensible as a route; it sees very little traffic. Parties can bypass the technical sections by staying lower on the west slope, avoiding the vertical sections but missing the ridge's technical interest.

Remmel is a classic Pasayten peak-bagging objective: a big, remote walk-up rather than a technical climb. Most parties backpack in via one of three trailheads (Thirtymile/Chewuch River Trail to Four Point Lake, the shorter but rougher Andrews Creek approach, or the Cathedral Driveway) and then follow an obvious boot path up open talus and meadow slopes to the broad summit.

Parties typically approach via Twisp River Road to either the Reynolds Creek drainage (shortest, most direct) or the Williams Creek trail, then climb open basins and snowfields on the southeast side of the peak to a saddle/notch below the summit. From there, a Class 2-3 gully leads to the ridge crest, followed by a short, somewhat exposed Class 3 scramble on solid granite to the true (southeast) summit.

moves.value: Longer alternative approaches traverse in from Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge, or from the west via Bridge Creek and Stehekin (the back way); all of them join the same southeast-side summit scramble.
moves.from: Longer alternative approaches traverse in from Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge, or from the west via Bridge Creek and Stehekin ('the back way'), but all eventually join the same southeast-side summit scramble rather than offering a genuinely distinct technical line.

beta_new: Sport-and-trad alpine climb on the south face with quality climbing on lower pitches transitioning to chossy rock mid-route before improving toward the summit. Bolted belay anchors on initial pitches; natural protection higher. The opening pitches below the roof are the route's best sections.

Once you have reached the summit of East Fury, you may continue to West Fury via this traverse. The traverse is a series of gendarmes and towers with a combination of scrambling and low 5th class rock. The descent off East Fury to the low saddle is on very loose Class 2-3 boulders. There are three towers you must climb up and over before making the final ascent to the summit of West Fury. A 50-60 meter rope is recommended at the very least for rappelling the 4th and low 5th class areas you have climbed.

value.text: A rope of at least 50-60 m, for rappelling the traverse.

moves.from: A 50-60 meter rope is recommended at the very least for rappelling the 4th and low 5th class areas you have climbed.

beta_new: Climbs the middle of Roan Wall via a 5.8 bolted slab approach pitch, a 5.4 approach pitch, sustained 5.9-5.10 edge and face pitches, and a 5.11a crux slab pitch (P7), finishing with mixed 5.9-5.10- climbing. All belays feature brand-new double-ring stainless-steel bolted anchors.

value.name: Martha's Place
value.notes: An enormously overhung boulder near the base of the wall that offers a good camp or bivy spot.

moves.from: An enormously overhung boulder (Martha's Place) sits near the base and offers a good camp/bivy spot.

beta_new: Features a pale slab approach pitch, face pitches with friction cruxes, corner climbing, sustained slab sections with crimpy holds, and finishes on a unique pitch combining an overlap crack with low-angle face climbing. Climbs the same very high-quality granite as the rest of Roan Wall.

moves.value: This route shares its approach and lower access with Center Stage. Before reaching Center Stage's start, traverse about 200 ft right to a pale slab between two obvious left-facing corners.
moves.from: Shares its approach and lower access with Center Stage; before reaching Center Stage's start, traverse about 200 feet right to a pale/white slab between two obvious left-facing corners.

beta_new: From the tarn, climb the loose scree slope (snow-covered in early season) north of the tarn to a gap in the southeast ridge, then turn left (north-west) and follow the ridge about a mile over several false summits — mostly class 2 walking with a few class 3 sections and a narrow, exposed crux just below the true summit.

moves.from: From the Robinson Creek Trailhead, follow the maintained Robinson Creek Trail north, cross Beauty Creek, and turn uphill onto the unmarked, unmaintained Beauty Creek Trail. Climb the brushy, steep Beauty Creek valley, cross a tributary around 5,200-5,260 ft, then ascend open meadow/scree to a small tarn at roughly 6,750-6,800 ft in a rocky basin.

beta_new: The finish of a longer cross-country ridge traverse rather than a stand-alone climb: from the Howard-Rock col, ascend Rock Mountain's northeast side (snow climbing and rock scrambling). Requires solid off-trail navigation and, in early season, snow-travel skills (an ice axe was necessary on a June ascent).

moves.from: , then descend via the South Ridge-East Slope to the Rock Lake basin and exit on the standard Rock Mountain Trail

beta_new: Pitch 1 (5.11+, ~25 ft) is a very thin traversing pitch where precise footwork is essential — a fall risks hitting the ledge below. Pitch 2 (5.10+) heads straight up the slab to the arete and tops out on Martha's Place. Fully bolted with 13 bolts total; the belay is split at a ledge partway up to prevent rope drag. Noted for excellent bolt placement.

A well-bolted, slightly steep climb on jug holds. Climbers can follow the bolt line straight to the chains, or after clipping the 5th bolt, traverse right onto a solid horn and back left for a mellower ledge variation.

Climb steeply up the hillside left (east) of the boulder field to gain the northwest ridge, follow it over Point 6315', transition onto the west ridge around 5,400 ft, and finish with a scramble up the summit ridge. In snow season, cliff bands along the ridge are typically turned via snow ramps.

moves.from: Park at a turnout across from a large boulder field on the northwest side of the mountain.

beta_new: Approach via the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail to Hannegan Pass, then follow an unmaintained climbers' trail south onto the Ruth Glacier and up easy snow to Ruth Mountain's summit. From Ruth, descend about 1,600 ft in two roughly 800-ft steps to the low saddle between Ruth and Icy, cross talus and glacier to a notch west of Icy's Northwest Spire near 6,500 ft, then climb roughly 500 ft of 2nd-3rd class terrain and a short 4th class summit gully to Icy Peak.

moves.from: The whole traverse is reversed to descend.

beta_new: Boston Basin sees less traffic and wider crevasse field on Quien Sabe Glacier compared to Sahale Glacier. Ascend left (north) side of Quien Sabe Glacier, watching for crevasses and selecting reasonable line—usually near center in steeper sections. Route between Sahale and Boston Peak summits (Sharkfin Tower is visible reference). Traverse south via col below the two peaks to reach Boston-Sahale Col. From col, traverse exposed snow to reach loose Class 3 summit scramble with persistent cornice into early summer. Final scramble is brief and loose.

moves.from: Boston Basin approach is steeper and rougher than Cascade Pass route. Trail is eroded and steep.

beta_new: Begin at Cascade Pass trailhead off Cascade River Road. The first 2.5 miles feature 35 gradual switchbacks gaining 1,500 ft. Transition from forest to alpine meadows. Sahale Glacier is small and not very active. Route weaves SW to N side of summit block. The short chimney feature (5.0) on pyramid's south side serves as main crux with exposure. Few pieces of rock pro useful for final moves. Most groups don't rope for scramble but protection is reasonable. Descend via rappel (or 5-rappel sequence for full descent) and traverse SE to loose rocks, then steep snow downclimb (40-45 degrees) or face-in descent, followed by scree traverse and plunge-stepping down gentle snowfield to camp.

Begins on the far right side of the main face; a few fourth-class moves lead to a starting ledge below the shield's roof. A quick boulder move leads to the obvious shield, which ends at a rap tree (~5 m). The route connects into the Traverse pitch. An old hex and Eiger USA biner were found stuck in the shield, suggesting an earlier unrecorded ascent; the route is credited to the Salish people who occupied this land long before rock climbing existed here.

From a high camp in the basin between Saska and the Fern Lake/Pyramid Mountain trail system, climbers cross talus, scree, or lingering snow slopes to gain the south ridge/col between Emerald and Saska peaks. From there a short but exposed class 3 scramble along a narrow, sometimes knife-edged ridge crest leads to the summit. Parties describe an obvious scree/rock gully on the right (west) side of the ridge, followed by a rising traverse (cairned) on the right side of the ridge, then final class 3 scrambling to the top. It is reported as the easiest and shortest of the Saska/Emerald/Cardinal trio's summit scrambles.

The Shield Wall is a prominent buttress visible from the Forest Service road below. The lower seven pitches climb generally modest fifth-class rock up the wall face, with a bolted first-pitch belay and two fixed bolts mid-pitch; the crux is a well-protected finger crack passing the second tower on the right. Above the wall, three 30m rappels alternate with about six more pitches (3rd class to 5.7) through the ridge's rock parapets and gendarmes to the summit. Expect to place only 1-5 pieces of protection on many pitches, with few opportunities to sling horns or blocks despite what older published descriptions suggest, and generally poor rock quality throughout.

Sentinel is most often climbed, probably almost exclusively climbed, by parties doing the famed Ptarmigan traverse. From a high camp near the LeConte–Sentinel col or on the South Cascade Glacier, parties ascend a slope to a moat on the right side of a ledge/ramp that crosses the south face; the ramp is not difficult but demands care throughout, and the final section to the summit is straightforward Class 2-3 scrambling on snow and rock. A steeper variation exists via the west ridge, involving a steep snow ramp near 7,400 ft and a short low-5th-class rock step into a gully below the final ridge crest — this is harder than the standard line and should be treated as an alternate finish, not the default.
Ascend the obvious southwest buttress north of the SW Couloir. Route features diverse climbing from cracks to slabs with good pro on harder sections and some exposed runouts on easier terrain.

Three short, low-fifth-class pitches follow the crest of the ridge from the notch at its base to the small summit, with huge exposure over the Boston Glacier for most of the climb. The rock is solid, high-quality granite and protection is generally good. It's a popular quick technical add-on to a Boston Basin trip (often combined with Sahale Peak or Boston Peak), but the glacier crossing and approach gully carry real objective hazard.

moves.value: Descend exactly the way you went up; a bit of temporary flagging can help you stay on line through the brushy class 3-4 terrain. Do not reuse old rappel webbing at the notch, since it is likely years old; bring your own to replace it.
moves.from: Descend exactly the way you went up (a bit of temporary flagging can help on the brushy class 3-4 terrain so you don't wander off-line), and do not reuse any old rappel webbing/tat found at the notch since it's likely to be years old — bring your own to replace it.

beta_new: From a high camp near the Squak Glacier, rope up and climb glaciated terrain through a documented crevasse maze (~8,700 ft) to the saddle below the Roman Wall, then traverse south of Baker's true summit and front-point up steep, often icy slopes to Sherman Peak's summit ridge, which can be corniced with large rime-ice knobs. The final short section to the actual summit is typically climbed unroped.

This is less a 'route up the peak' than the technical crux feature of Sherpa Peak: a free-standing granite pillar near the true summit. Parties typically combine it with the Class 3-4 ridge traverse to Sherpa's main summit. The crux move onto the pedestal has historically been done either by shoulder-standing a partner or by throwing/lassoing a rope over the pedestal's point; from there, bolt-protected friction slab gains the flat top, from which a single aging bolt is used to rappel back down.

From a basin camp around 6,800 ft, follow the east ridge toward the summit; cairns and fixed slings/webbing along the ridge aid route-finding. The route passes around the balanced rock from the north side, which can involve a sketchy traverse over snow or wet rock in early season. The balanced-rock move itself is a shoulder-stand or rope-throw over a pedestal point to gain its east side, then bolt-protected friction climbing to the top, rated 5.7, with a rappel bolt atop.
